title: AP Biology — Chapter 13 (meiosis and heredity)
source: Carter's Ch 13 guide: her slide deck slides 1-51, his spoken priority list, plus the Mendel/Hardy-Weinberg half of the Fri 11/13 quiz. Refresh this file when the unit changes.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte (2n = 46) completes meiosis I normally, forming a secondary oocyte and a first polar body. The secondary oocyte receives 23 chromosomes. What is the chromosome number and ploidy of the first polar body?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes; haploid
distractors: 46 chromosomes; diploid
23 chromosomes; diploid
46 chromosomes; haploid
questions.why: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, so both the secondary oocyte and first polar body receive one chromosome from each pair and are haploid. The 46/23 confusion treats the polar body as a diploid somatic cell.
options: 23 chromosomes; haploid
23 chromosomes; diploid
46 chromosomes; haploid
46 chromosomes; diploid

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human cell shows 47 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome. Which description of this karyotype is correct?
questions.correct: It has 44 autosomes and three sex chromosomes.
distractors: It has 45 autosomes and two sex chromosomes.
It has 46 autosomes and one sex chromosome.
It has 22 autosomes and 25 sex chromosomes.
questions.why: The 47 chromosomes consist of 22 autosome pairs (44 autosomes) plus XXY, so there are three sex chromosomes. A common error is to count the extra chromosome as an autosome instead of recognizing the XXY sex-chromosome set.
options: It has 45 autosomes and two sex chromosomes.
It has 44 autosomes and three sex chromosomes.
It has 22 autosomes and 25 sex chromosomes.
It has 46 autosomes and one sex chromosome.

questions.stem: A diploid organism has 2n = 8. A cell from this organism enters meiosis and is examined in prophase I, after DNA replication. How many homologous pairs and how many chromatids are present in that cell?
questions.correct: 4 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
distractors: 8 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
8 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
questions.why: With 2n = 8 there are four homologous pairs, and replication gives each of the eight chromosomes two chromatids, for 16. The 8-pair choice mistakes individual chromosomes for pairs.
options: 8 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
8 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids

questions.stem: During prophase I, a single crossover occurs between two non-sister chromatids of one homologous pair. After meiosis II, what is the recombinant content of the four chromatids that came from that pair?
questions.correct: Two chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles; two remain nonrecombinant.
distractors: All four chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles.
No chromatids are recombinant because sister chromatids are identical.
All four chromatids carry only paternal alleles.
questions.why: A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids only, so two of the four chromatids become recombinant while the other two stay parental. The all-four choice assumes crossing over affects every chromatid in the pair.
options: No chromatids are recombinant because sister chromatids are identical.
All four chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles.
All four chromatids carry only paternal alleles.
Two chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles; two remain nonrecombinant.

questions.stem: A moss sporophyte is diploid and undergoes meiosis to produce spores. A human germ cell is also diploid and undergoes meiosis. How do the products differ in these two life cycles?
questions.correct: Moss meiosis produces haploid spores that grow into a gametophyte; human meiosis produces haploid gametes directly.
distractors: Moss meiosis produces diploid gametes; human meiosis produces haploid spores.
Both produce haploid spores that divide by mitosis into gametes.
Both produce diploid gametes that fuse to form a haploid zygote.
questions.why: In plants, meiosis yields spores and the haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis; in animals, meiosis yields gametes directly. The spore/gamete mix-up is the common plant-versus-animal life-cycle misconception.
options: Moss meiosis produces haploid spores that grow into a gametophyte; human meiosis produces haploid gametes directly.
Moss meiosis produces diploid gametes; human meiosis produces haploid spores.
Both produce haploid spores that divide by mitosis into gametes.
Both produce diploid gametes that fuse to form a haploid zygote.

questions.stem: One human primary spermatocyte (2n = 46) completes meiosis normally. How many sperm are produced, and how many chromosomes does each sperm carry?
questions.correct: Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes
distractors: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
One sperm, with 23 chromosomes
questions.why: Meiosis of one primary spermatocyte yields four haploid sperm, each with 23 chromosomes. The 46-chromosome choice confuses the diploid primary spermatocyte with its haploid products.
options: One sperm, with 23 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes

questions.stem: In a human male, the X and Y chromosomes differ in size and gene content. What happens to them during meiosis I?
questions.correct: They pair as homologs and separate in anaphase I.
distractors: They do not pair, so both usually go to the same sperm.
They replicate again during meiosis II before separating.
They separate as sister chromatids in anaphase II.
questions.why: X and Y share a small homologous region that allows them to pair and separate like other homologs in meiosis I. The non-pairing choice assumes different sex chromosomes cannot be homologs.
options: They do not pair, so both usually go to the same sperm.
They separate as sister chromatids in anaphase II.
They pair as homologs and separate in anaphase I.
They replicate again during meiosis II before separating.

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II. A sperm enters and triggers completion of meiosis II. What is the immediate result for the oocyte's chromosomes?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids separate, and a second polar body is released.
distractors: Homologous chromosomes separate, and a first polar body is released.
DNA replicates again before the chromosomes separate.
The sperm and oocyte nuclei fuse before meiosis II finishes.
questions.why: Meiosis II resumes at fertilization, separating sister chromatids and producing the ovum plus a second polar body. The homolog-separation choice confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: Homologous chromosomes separate, and a first polar body is released.
DNA replicates again before the chromosomes separate.
The sperm and oocyte nuclei fuse before meiosis II finishes.
Sister chromatids separate, and a second polar body is released.

questions.stem: A technician prepares a human karyotype by blocking cells at metaphase, staining the chromosomes, and arranging them in pairs. Why is metaphase chosen for this procedure?
questions.correct: Chromosomes are condensed and can be seen as distinct bodies.
distractors: Homologous chromosomes have just separated into different cells.
Sister chromatids have just separated and are no longer attached.
Chromosomes are in chromatin form and easier to spread.
questions.why: At metaphase, replicated chromosomes are tightly condensed, making them visible and measurable for pairing. The anaphase choice is wrong because separation would leave each cell with only one of each homolog.
options: Chromosomes are condensed and can be seen as distinct bodies.
Chromosomes are in chromatin form and easier to spread.
Sister chromatids have just separated and are no longer attached.
Homologous chromosomes have just separated into different cells.

questions.stem: Human oogenesis produces one large ovum and small polar bodies from a single primary oocyte. What explains this unequal division?
questions.correct: Cytoplasm is partitioned unequally, so one cell retains most of the resources for the zygote.
distractors: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized.
Meiosis II occurs only in the ovum, not in polar bodies.
Polar bodies contain no chromosomes.
questions.why: Unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis concentrates cytoplasm in the ovum; polar bodies are haploid byproducts. The no-chromosomes choice confuses small size with lacking genetic material.
options: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized.
Cytoplasm is partitioned unequally, so one cell retains most of the resources for the zygote.
Meiosis II occurs only in the ovum, not in polar bodies.
Polar bodies contain no chromosomes.

questions.stem: A student's lab notebook reads: "Crossing over in prophase I creates new alleles, which is why no two gametes are alike." Which statement best corrects this claim?
questions.correct: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles that were already present in the parent cell.
distractors: Crossing over exchanges segments between sister chromatids, which is why each resulting chromatid carries alleles that the parent cell never had.
Crossing over alters the chromosome number of the products, so gametes end up carrying allele combinations absent from the parent cell.
Crossing over generates brand-new alleles at each locus, while independent assortment only shuffles the chromosomes that carry them.
questions.why: Crossing over is a physical swap of homologous segments, so it reshuffles existing alleles rather than creating them; mutation is the source of new alleles. The distractors exploit the common misconception that recombination itself invents alleles.
options: Crossing over exchanges segments between sister chromatids, which is why each resulting chromatid carries alleles that the parent cell never had.
Crossing over alters the chromosome number of the products, so gametes end up carrying allele combinations absent from the parent cell.
Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles that were already present in the parent cell.
Crossing over generates brand-new alleles at each locus, while independent assortment only shuffles the chromosomes that carry them.

questions.stem: In a primary spermatocyte, both sister chromatids of one homolog of chromosome 4 are labeled with a fluorescent dye; the other homolog is unlabeled. The cell completes meiosis normally with no crossing over. How many of the four sperm carry the label?
questions.correct: Two sperm, because the labeled homolog goes to one secondary spermatocyte and its sister chromatids separate into two sperm.
distractors: One sperm, because only one chromatid of the labeled homolog enters a sperm.
Four sperm, because the label is copied to all chromatids during meiosis.
Zero sperm, because the labeled homolog is degraded during meiosis I.
questions.why: The labeled homolog segregates from its partner in meiosis I, then its sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, giving two labeled sperm. The one-sperm choice confuses homolog separation with sister-chromatid separation.
options: Four sperm, because the label is copied to all chromatids during meiosis.
One sperm, because only one chromatid of the labeled homolog enters a sperm.
Zero sperm, because the labeled homolog is degraded during meiosis I.
Two sperm, because the labeled homolog goes to one secondary spermatocyte and its sister chromatids separate into two sperm.

questions.stem: A diploid cell with 2n = 4 is in anaphase I. Cytokinesis has not occurred, so all chromosomes are still in one cell. How many chromosomes are present in that single cell?
questions.correct: Four chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
distractors: Two chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Eight chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
Four chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
questions.why: Homologs have separated toward opposite poles but remain in one cytoplasm, and sister chromatids are still attached, so the cell has four duplicated chromosomes. Counting chromatids as chromosomes gives eight.
options: Four chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Two chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Eight chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
Four chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.

questions.stem: A karyotype prepared from a human shows 45 chromosomes, including one X chromosome and no Y chromosome. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The individual is female with monosomy X, a condition called Turner syndrome.
distractors: The individual is male with Klinefelter syndrome.
The individual is a normal female with 22 autosome pairs.
The individual is female with trisomy X.
questions.why: One X and no Y indicates female, and 45 total chromosomes means one chromosome is missing, matching Turner syndrome (45,X). The distractors swap sex-chromosome constitution or chromosome number.
options: The individual is female with trisomy X.
The individual is female with monosomy X, a condition called Turner syndrome.
The individual is a normal female with 22 autosome pairs.
The individual is male with Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: At birth, a human female's primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I. Each primary oocyte has 46 chromosomes. What is the chromatid content of one such oocyte?
questions.correct: 92 chromatids, because each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids.
distractors: 46 chromatids, because each chromosome has one chromatid before meiosis.
23 chromatids, because meiosis I has already reduced the chromosome number.
92 chromosomes, because DNA replication doubles the chromosome count.
questions.why: The oocyte is diploid and has already replicated its DNA, so each of the 46 chromosomes is duplicated into two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids but still 46 chromosomes. The last distractor assumes replication doubles chromosome number.
options: 23 chromatids, because meiosis I has already reduced the chromosome number.
92 chromosomes, because DNA replication doubles the chromosome count.
92 chromatids, because each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids.
46 chromatids, because each chromosome has one chromatid before meiosis.

questions.stem: A sperm carries two copies of chromosome 7. At a locus near the centromere, one copy has allele A and the other has allele a; no crossing over occurred near that locus. Which meiotic error most likely produced this sperm?
questions.correct: Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes carrying A and a failed to separate.
distractors: Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because sister chromatids carrying A and a failed to separate.
Crossing over in prophase I, because it exchanged A for a between homologs.
Fertilization by two sperm, because each sperm contributed a chromosome 7.
questions.why: The two copies are homologs with different alleles, so they should have separated in meiosis I; meiosis II nondisjunction would produce two identical sister chromatids, not A and a. The meiosis II choice ignores that sisters are identical at that locus.
options: Crossing over in prophase I, because it exchanged A for a between homologs.
Fertilization by two sperm, because each sperm contributed a chromosome 7.
Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because sister chromatids carrying A and a failed to separate.
Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes carrying A and a failed to separate.

questions.stem: A drug blocks chiasma formation in a primary spermatocyte, but homologs still align at metaphase I. What is the most likely consequence for the resulting sperm?
questions.correct: Homologs may segregate randomly, producing sperm with abnormal chromosome numbers.
distractors: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so each sperm receives duplicated chromosomes.
DNA replication fails, so each sperm receives half the normal DNA.
Crossing over increases, so all sperm become genetically identical.
questions.why: Chiasmata normally hold homologs together so they orient and separate correctly; without them, homologs can missegregate, causing aneuploid sperm. The distractors confuse chiasmata with sister-chromatid cohesion or replication.
options: Homologs may segregate randomly, producing sperm with abnormal chromosome numbers.
Crossing over increases, so all sperm become genetically identical.
Sister chromatids cannot separate, so each sperm receives duplicated chromosomes.
DNA replication fails, so each sperm receives half the normal DNA.

questions.stem: Colchicine prevents spindle microtubules from forming. A primary oocyte treated with colchicine enters meiosis. What is the most direct effect on chromosome segregation?
questions.correct: Homologs and sister chromatids cannot be pulled apart, so no normal haploid products form.
distractors: Crossing over cannot occur, so homologs remain genetically identical.
DNA replication is blocked, so chromosomes remain unreplicated.
Sister chromatids separate but homologs remain paired, producing diploid gametes.
questions.why: Spindle fibers move chromosomes; without them, segregation fails regardless of crossing over or replication. The distractors wrongly link the spindle to crossing over, replication, or a selective separation.
options: Crossing over cannot occur, so homologs remain genetically identical.
Homologs and sister chromatids cannot be pulled apart, so no normal haploid products form.
DNA replication is blocked, so chromosomes remain unreplicated.
Sister chromatids separate but homologs remain paired, producing diploid gametes.

questions.stem: A human egg with 23 chromosomes is fertilized by two sperm at the same time, and both sperm fuse with the egg. Each sperm has 23 chromosomes. What is the chromosome number of the resulting zygote?
questions.correct: 69 chromosomes, because three haploid sets combine.
distractors: 46 chromosomes, because two sperm replace the missing second gamete.
92 chromosomes, because each sperm doubles after fusion.
23 chromosomes, because the egg's chromosomes are discarded.
questions.why: Fertilization normally combines one haploid egg and one haploid sperm; two sperm add two more haploid sets to the egg's set, giving three sets (69). The distractors miscount the sets or assume chromosome loss or doubling.
options: 92 chromosomes, because each sperm doubles after fusion.
46 chromosomes, because two sperm replace the missing second gamete.
69 chromosomes, because three haploid sets combine.
23 chromosomes, because the egg's chromosomes are discarded.

questions.stem: A student claims that crossing over between sister chromatids during prophase I increases genetic variation. Why is this claim incorrect?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids are identical copies, so exchanging segments between them does not create new allele combinations.
distractors: Sister chromatids are not present in prophase I, so crossing over cannot occur then.
Crossing over between sister chromatids creates new alleles at the break points.
Crossing over only occurs between nonhomologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids.
questions.why: Crossing over generates variation only when non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange different alleles; sister chromatids carry the same alleles, so the exchange is genetically invisible. The distractor about new alleles confuses recombination with mutation.
options: Crossing over only occurs between nonhomologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids.
Crossing over between sister chromatids creates new alleles at the break points.
Sister chromatids are not present in prophase I, so crossing over cannot occur then.
Sister chromatids are identical copies, so exchanging segments between them does not create new allele combinations.

questions.stem: A table gives human cell counts. Which row is inconsistent with normal cell-cycle or meiotic behavior? G1 somatic cell: 46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids. G2 somatic cell: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids. Secondary spermatocyte: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids. Spermatid: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids.
questions.correct: Spermatid, because a spermatid has 23 chromosomes but each chromosome should be a single chromatid.
distractors: G1 somatic cell, because it should have 92 chromatids.
G2 somatic cell, because it should have 46 chromatids.
Secondary spermatocyte, because it should have 46 chromosomes.
questions.why: After meiosis II, spermatids contain 23 unduplicated chromosomes (23 chromatids); 46 chromatids would mean each chromosome is still duplicated. The other rows match expected counts.
options: Spermatid, because a spermatid has 23 chromosomes but each chromosome should be a single chromatid.
G2 somatic cell, because it should have 46 chromatids.
Secondary spermatocyte, because it should have 46 chromosomes.
G1 somatic cell, because it should have 92 chromatids.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a normal human male is arranged in 23 pairs. A student places a label on every chromosome that is not an X or a Y. How many labels are placed?
questions.correct: 44 labels, because there are 22 autosome pairs.
distractors: 46 labels, because all chromosomes are autosomes in a male.
23 labels, because autosomes are counted by pairs rather than individually.
45 labels, because only the Y chromosome is excluded.
questions.why: Autosomes are all chromosomes except sex chromosomes; a male has 22 autosome pairs (44 chromosomes) plus X and Y. The distractors count sex chromosomes as autosomes or count pairs instead of chromosomes.
options: 46 labels, because all chromosomes are autosomes in a male.
44 labels, because there are 22 autosome pairs.
45 labels, because only the Y chromosome is excluded.
23 labels, because autosomes are counted by pairs rather than individually.

questions.stem: A diploid organism has four homologous pairs. Assuming independent assortment and no crossing over, what fraction of its gametes receives the paternal homolog from every pair?
questions.why: Each of the four pairs independently gives a 1/2 chance of the paternal homolog, so (1/2)^4 = 1/16; 1/4 confuses the number of pairs with the probability per pair.

questions.stem: A human karyotype is prepared from a cell arrested at metaphase, so each of the 46 chromosomes is duplicated. How many DNA molecules are displayed in the entire karyotype?
questions.why: At metaphase each chromosome has two sister chromatids, each one DNA molecule, giving 46 × 2 = 92; 46 counts chromosomes rather than chromatids.

questions.stem: A technician tries to arrange chromosomes from a normal human sperm into homologous pairs for a karyotype but cannot. What best explains this failure?
questions.correct: A sperm is haploid, so it carries only one chromosome from each homologous pair.
distractors: A sperm has no chromosomes until fertilization, when they are supplied by the egg.
A sperm's chromosomes are all sex chromosomes, so autosomes cannot be paired.
A sperm has homologous pairs but they are too condensed to recognize.
questions.why: Meiosis reduces the chromosome set to one of each homolog, so a sperm lacks the partner chromosome needed for pairing; the first distractor reverses fertilization's role.
options: A sperm is haploid, so it carries only one chromosome from each homologous pair.
A sperm has homologous pairs but they are too condensed to recognize.
A sperm's chromosomes are all sex chromosomes, so autosomes cannot be paired.
A sperm has no chromosomes until fertilization, when they are supplied by the egg.

questions.stem: A human primary spermatocyte contains one X and one Y chromosome. It completes meiosis normally, producing four sperm. How many of those sperm carry an X chromosome?
questions.correct: Two
distractors: Zero
One
Four
questions.why: The X and Y homologs separate in meiosis I, so two secondary spermatocytes—and their two sperm—receive the X; choosing one assumes sex chromosomes segregate only after meiosis II.
options: Zero
Two
Four
One

questions.stem: A moss gametophyte is haploid and produces gametes by mitosis. A human produces gametes by meiosis. Which comparison of the resulting gametes is correct?
questions.correct: Moss gametes are genetically identical to the gametophyte apart from mutation, while human gametes vary because meiosis shuffles homologs.
distractors: Moss gametes are diploid, while human gametes are haploid because meiosis halves the chromosome number.
Moss gametes vary because mitosis separates homologs, while human gametes are identical to the parent cell.
Both moss and human gametes are produced by meiosis, but moss gametes are larger and therefore diploid.
questions.why: Mitosis in a haploid gametophyte copies the same set, whereas meiosis in humans makes variable haploid gametes; calling moss gametes diploid ignores that the gametophyte is already haploid.
options: Moss gametes are diploid, while human gametes are haploid because meiosis halves the chromosome number.
Moss gametes vary because mitosis separates homologs, while human gametes are identical to the parent cell.
Moss gametes are genetically identical to the gametophyte apart from mutation, while human gametes vary because meiosis shuffles homologs.
Both moss and human gametes are produced by meiosis, but moss gametes are larger and therefore diploid.

questions.stem: A human egg with 23 chromosomes fuses with a normal sperm, forming a zygote. Immediately after fusion, before any DNA replication, how many chromosomes and DNA molecules does the zygote contain?
questions.correct: 46 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules
distractors: 46 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
23 chromosomes and 23 DNA molecules
92 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
questions.why: Fertilization restores 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes, each then a single DNA molecule before S phase; 92 DNA molecules would require replication already.
options: 92 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
46 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
23 chromosomes and 23 DNA molecules
46 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules

questions.stem: In a diploid species, one cell is in anaphase II and, before cytokinesis, contains 24 chromosomes. What is the diploid number of this species?
questions.why: At anaphase II sister chromatids separate, so the 24 chromosomes in that cell represent two copies of the haploid set of 12; thus n = 12 and 2n = 24.

questions.stem: A mutant diploid organism is found to have only one set of chromosomes (n = 8) instead of two. It cannot complete meiosis. What is the most direct reason?
questions.correct: It lacks homologous pairs that must synapse and separate in meiosis I.
distractors: It cannot replicate DNA because replication requires two chromosome sets.
Its cells cannot enter mitosis, so meiosis never begins.
It has no centromeres, so sister chromatids cannot attach to spindle fibers.
questions.why: Meiosis I requires homologs to pair and then segregate, and a haploid set has no homolog partners; the replication distractor falsely claims S phase needs two sets.
options: It cannot replicate DNA because replication requires two chromosome sets.
It lacks homologous pairs that must synapse and separate in meiosis I.
It has no centromeres, so sister chromatids cannot attach to spindle fibers.
Its cells cannot enter mitosis, so meiosis never begins.

questions.stem: A tetraploid plant has 4n = 32. It undergoes meiosis to produce gametes. How many chromosomes does each gamete carry?
questions.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number from the tetraploid sporophyte, so gametes receive 32/2 = 16; 8 would be a haploid set of the original diploid, not the tetraploid.

questions.stem: A child's karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with no visible structural abnormalities. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The karyotype does not rule out a single-gene mutation causing the child's disorder.
distractors: The child cannot have a genetic disorder because all chromosomes are present.
The child must have an extra copy of a gene that karyotyping cannot detect.
The child's gametes will all have 23 chromosomes regardless of the child's genotype.
questions.why: Karyotypes reveal chromosome number and large structure, not DNA sequence, so a point mutation can still cause disease; the first distractor treats a normal karyotype as a complete genetic screen.
options: The child must have an extra copy of a gene that karyotyping cannot detect.
The child cannot have a genetic disorder because all chromosomes are present.
The child's gametes will all have 23 chromosomes regardless of the child's genotype.
The karyotype does not rule out a single-gene mutation causing the child's disorder.

questions.stem: A normal human egg is produced. How many autosomes and sex chromosomes does it carry?
questions.correct: 22 autosomes and one X chromosome
distractors: 23 autosomes and one X chromosome
22 autosomes and one Y chromosome
44 autosomes and one X chromosome
questions.why: A human egg is haploid for 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome, and eggs carry X rather than Y; 23 autosomes would incorrectly include a sex chromosome as an autosome.
options: 22 autosomes and one X chromosome
44 autosomes and one X chromosome
23 autosomes and one X chromosome
22 autosomes and one Y chromosome

questions.stem: A human karyotype shows 23 pairs of chromosomes. Which statement about that display is correct?
options: Twenty-two pairs are autosomes, and the members of a pair are homologs matched in length, shape and gene loci, one inherited from each parent.
All 23 pairs are autosomes, and each pair is a set of sister chromatids.
Twenty-three pairs of autosomes are present plus a separate pair of sex chromosomes.
The pairing proves the cell is haploid, because each chromosome has one partner.
questions.why: Humans carry 22 autosome pairs plus one sex pair; homologs match in length and shape and carry the same loci, one copy per parent.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 6 has finished meiosis I and its two daughters are at metaphase II. How many chromosomes and chromatids does each daughter hold?
options: 6 chromosomes and 6 chromatids, because the set has not been halved yet.
3 chromosomes and 6 chromatids, because each chromosome is still two sister chromatids.
3 chromosomes and 3 chromatids, because the sisters have already separated.
6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids, because the DNA was copied after meiosis I.
questions.why: Meiosis I halves the set to n = 3 but leaves each chromosome doubled, so 3 chromosomes carry 6 chromatids until anaphase II.

questions.stem: At metaphase II, the two sister chromatids of a chromosome attach to microtubules from opposite poles. Why are those sisters not genetically identical?
options: Because DNA replication in meiosis II introduces new mutations into one sister.
Because the sisters separated during anaphase I and then rejoined.
Because crossing over in prophase I exchanged segments between nonsister chromatids, so the sisters carry different allele combinations.
Because maternal and paternal chromosomes fused at the metaphase II plate.
questions.why: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between nonsister chromatids in prophase I, so each sister carries a mixed set of alleles.

questions.stem: During anaphase I the homologs separate while sister chromatids stay together. What makes that possible?
options: Cohesin is cleaved at the centromeres first, then along the arms in anaphase II.
Cohesin is not involved; the spindle pulls homologs apart directly.
Cohesin is fully degraded at the end of metaphase I, releasing sisters immediately.
Cohesin is cleaved along the chromosome arms, while centromeric cohesin stays intact until anaphase II.
questions.why: Arm cohesin is cut in anaphase I to free the homologs; centromeric cohesin persists so sisters travel together until anaphase II.

questions.stem: Why is there no DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II?
options: Because the chromosomes were already replicated in interphase, and a second replication would double the genome again.
Because meiosis II is not a real division and requires no new DNA.
Because replication happens during telophase I and is too fast to observe.
Because each daughter cell replicates its DNA during prophase II.
questions.why: One S phase precedes meiosis I; replicating again before meiosis II would give each gamete twice the DNA it should carry.

questions.stem: Why are all four products of meiosis genetically distinct from one another?
options: Because each product receives a different number of chromosomes.
Independent assortment gives different combinations of homologs, and crossing over puts different alleles on the chromatids.
Because mutation occurs in every one of the four daughter cells.
Because sister chromatids are identical and separate randomly at anaphase II.
questions.why: Assortment mixes which homologs travel together and crossing over mixes alleles along each chromosome, so no two products match.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly states what separates in each meiotic anaphase?
options: Anaphase I separates sister chromatids; anaphase II separates homologs.
Both anaphases separate homologs, which is why the set halves twice.
Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes; anaphase II separates sister chromatids.
Anaphase I separates sister chromatids of each homolog simultaneously.
questions.why: Meiosis I is the reductional division that pulls homologs apart; meiosis II is the equational division that splits sisters.

questions.stem: Two homologous pairs line up at metaphase I. What does independent assortment predict about the resulting gametes?
options: Only two gamete types are possible, because the pairs travel together.
Gametes carry both homologs of each pair until meiosis II.
Two gamete types form, with the recombinant types appearing only after crossing over.
Four gamete types are possible, because each pair's orientation is independent of the other pair's.
questions.why: Each pair orients randomly and independently, so two pairs produce 2^2 = 4 equally likely gamete combinations.

questions.stem: What happens during synapsis in prophase I?
options: Homologs pair along their lengths, held by the synaptonemal complex, and nonsister chromatids exchange corresponding segments.
Sister chromatids separate at the centromere and begin moving to the poles.
Homologs line up single file at the metaphase plate.
The nuclear envelope re-forms around each haploid set.
questions.why: Synapsis is the physical pairing of homologs in prophase I; crossing over occurs within that paired structure and creates chiasmata.

questions.stem: A chromosome in a gamete carries alleles that came from both of the student's grandparents on the same side of the family. What produced that?
options: Independent assortment at metaphase I, which mixes whole chromosomes.
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids in prophase I, which makes recombinant chromosomes.
Random fertilization, which combines gametes from two parents.
Nondisjunction, which changes how chromosomes are distributed.
questions.why: A single chromosome carrying DNA from both homologs is the signature of crossing over; assortment only mixes intact chromosomes.

questions.stem: The number of gamete combinations from independent assortment is 2^n, where n is the haploid number. For humans, what does that give?
options: 2^46, more than 70 trillion combinations.
23^2, or 529 combinations.
2^23, more than 8 million combinations.
2 x 23, or 46 combinations.
questions.why: n = 23 in humans, so independent assortment alone yields 2^23, about 8.4 million different gametes.

questions.stem: Why does random fertilization increase variation even though it adds no new alleles?
options: Because fertilization creates new alleles by recombining DNA inside the zygote.
Because the sperm selects which of the egg's chromosomes will be retained.
Because fertilization doubles the chromosome number of each gamete.
Because any sperm can fuse with any ovum, so the combination of two already-varied gametes multiplies the possibilities.
questions.why: Fertilization does not create alleles; it pairs one of millions of sperm with one of millions of eggs, multiplying combinations.

questions.stem: One primary spermatocyte yields four sperm with 24, 24, 22 and 22 chromosomes (human). Which division failed?
options: Meiosis I, because all four gametes are abnormal and the error appears in both products of the first division.
Meiosis II, because only one of the two secondary cells produced abnormal gametes.
Mitosis after fertilization, because the counts are unequal.
Crossing over, because recombination changed the chromosome counts.
questions.why: A meiosis I nondisjunction sends both homologs to one pole, so both secondary cells inherit the error and all four gametes are abnormal.

questions.stem: Four gametes carry 24, 22, 23 and 23 chromosomes. Which event explains this pattern?
options: Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because all four products differ from 23.
Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because only one of the two secondary cells divided abnormally.
Failure of crossing over, because recombination preserves the count.
Failure of cytokinesis in meiosis I, because the cells never separated.
questions.why: When exactly two of four gametes are abnormal and the other two are normal, the error was confined to one secondary cell at meiosis II.

questions.stem: An n+1 gamete fuses with a normal n gamete. What is the result, and how does it differ from an n-1 gamete fusing?
options: A monosomic zygote; an n-1 gamete gives trisomy, which is usually viable.
A haploid zygote; an n-1 gamete gives a diploid zygote.
A trisomic zygote with three copies of one chromosome; an n-1 gamete gives monosomy, which is usually lethal.
A polyploid zygote with two extra sets; an n-1 gamete removes one whole set.
questions.why: n+1 plus n gives three copies (trisomy, as in trisomy 21); n-1 plus n leaves one copy (monosomy), which is usually not viable.

questions.stem: A sperm carries a Y chromosome. What follows for the zygote, and what was the sperm's own chromosome content?
options: The zygote will be XX and female, and the sperm carried two diploid sets.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried 46 chromosomes.
The zygote's sex cannot be predicted, because the egg may also carry a Y.
The zygote will be XY and male, and the sperm carried a single haploid set of 23.
questions.why: Eggs always carry X, so a Y-bearing sperm produces an XY male; gametes are haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which statement about gametes in animals is correct?
options: They are the only haploid cells, and they do not divide again before fertilization.
They are diploid, and they divide by mitosis after meiosis.
They are haploid and divide by meiosis a second time before fusing.
They are haploid in males but diploid in females.
questions.why: Gametes are the sole haploid cells in animals; they fuse rather than divide, and the zygote then grows by mitosis.

questions.stem: Two chromosomes form a homologous pair. Which description is correct?
options: They carry identical alleles at every locus, which is why they pair.
They carry the same genes at the same loci, matched in length and shape, but may carry different alleles.
They carry different genes entirely, and pairing matches them by size only.
They are the two sister chromatids produced when the chromosome replicated.
questions.why: Homologs share loci and structure, one from each parent; the alleles at those loci can differ, which is what makes crossing over matter.

questions.stem: Which set of events occurs in meiosis but never in mitosis?
options: Chromosome condensation, spindle formation and sister chromatid separation.
DNA replication in interphase and cytokinesis at the end of division.
Synapsis with crossing over in prophase I, homologous pairs at the metaphase plate, and homolog separation in anaphase I.
Nuclear envelope breakdown and kinetochore attachment to microtubules.
questions.why: Those three events are the reason meiosis reduces the set; everything else on the list is shared machinery.

questions.stem: What do haploid and diploid actually describe?
options: The number of chromatids per chromosome, one versus two.
The amount of DNA in the nucleus, 2C versus 4C.
Whether the cell is a gamete or a somatic cell, regardless of chromosome number.
The number of chromosome SETS: one of each chromosome versus two of each.
questions.why: Diploid means two sets and haploid means one set; a replicated haploid cell still has two chromatids per chromosome, which is a different measure.

questions.stem: A human gamete carries 23 chromosomes. What is that set, and what happens to the number at fertilization?
options: 22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization restores 2n = 46.
22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization restores 2n = 23.
23 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome, and fertilization gives 48.
46 chromosomes, half of which are degraded at fertilization.
questions.why: n = 23 means 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome; adding the other gamete's set gives 46, the diploid number.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of crossing an individual of unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive partner?
options: It doubles the number of offspring, which makes ratios easier to read.
The recessive partner contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring phenotypes reveal the unknown genotype.
It converts recessive alleles into dominant ones in the offspring.
It prevents crossing over, so linkage can be measured directly.
questions.why: Because the tester contributes only recessive alleles, any dominant offspring must have received the dominant allele from the unknown parent.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt), and all 80 offspring are tall. What is the best conclusion?
options: The tall parent is heterozygous (Tt), because half the offspring should be dwarf.
The tall parent's genotype cannot be determined from any offspring counts.
The tall parent is homozygous dominant (TT), because no recessive offspring appeared.
The cross shows that height and flower color are linked.
questions.why: A heterozygote crossed to tt yields roughly 1:1; with 80 offspring all dominant, the parent is almost certainly TT.

questions.stem: A double heterozygote is testcrossed and yields four phenotypic classes in roughly equal numbers. What does that establish?
options: The two genes are completely linked, which is why all four classes appear.
One gene is epistatic to the other, which masks one class.
The parent was homozygous for both traits, which is why the ratio is even.
The two genes assort independently, which is why the 1:1:1:1 ratio appears.
questions.why: Equal numbers of all four classes is the signature of independent assortment; complete linkage would keep only the two parental classes.

questions.stem: Two heterozygotes for unlinked genes are crossed. What offspring ratio is expected?
options: 9:3:3:1 across the four phenotype combinations.
1:1:1:1, because each gene assorts independently.
3:1, because only one gene is segregating.
1:2:1, because each genotype appears once.
questions.why: A 9:3:3:1 ratio is the product of two independent 3:1 monohybrid ratios.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what does the frequency of the recessive PHENOTYPE give you directly?
options: q, which you square to get the recessive allele frequency.
q^2, which you square-root to get the recessive allele frequency q.
2pq, which you halve to get the heterozygote frequency.
p^2, which you subtract from 1 to get q.
questions.why: Only recessive homozygotes show the recessive phenotype, so their frequency is q^2; rooting it gives q.

questions.stem: In a population at equilibrium, 16 percent of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What fraction is heterozygous?
options: 0.16, because the recessive phenotype frequency equals the heterozygote frequency.
0.24, because q times p gives the heterozygote fraction.
0.36, because p squared gives the heterozygote fraction.
questions.why: q^2 = 0.16 gives q = 0.4 and p = 0.6, so heterozygotes = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48.

questions.stem: A beetle population of 1,000 is reduced to 20 individuals on an isolated island. Which assumption of Hardy-Weinberg is most likely to fail first?
options: Random mating, because small populations always mate assortatively.
No mutation, because small populations mutate more often per individual.
No gene flow, because islands cannot exchange migrants at all.
Large population size, because allele frequencies shift by chance in a small population.
questions.why: Genetic drift is the consequence of small N: sampling error moves allele frequencies regardless of fitness.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a population to be at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
options: Allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation because no evolutionary force is acting.
Every individual has the same genotype, so no variation remains.
The dominant allele is being selected for, so its frequency rises.
Mutation and selection are exactly balanced, holding the recessive allele constant.
questions.why: Equilibrium means the frequencies are stable; it is the null model against which real change is measured.

questions.stem: What is the correct division of labor between mutation and sexual reproduction?
options: Meiosis creates new alleles; mutation only redistributes them among offspring.
Mutation originates new alleles; meiosis and fertilization redistribute the alleles that already exist.
Both create new alleles, which is why sexual populations mutate faster.
Neither creates variation; variation comes only from the environment.
questions.why: Mutation is the only source of new alleles; assortment, crossing over and fertilization reshuffle them into new combinations.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a source of variation to its stage?
options: Independent assortment in prophase I, crossing over at metaphase I, mutation at fertilization.
Crossing over in anaphase I, independent assortment at anaphase II, mutation at fusion.
Crossing over in prophase I, independent assortment at metaphase I, random fertilization at fusion.
Random fertilization in prophase I, crossing over at metaphase II, assortment at fusion.
questions.why: Crossing over is a prophase I event, assortment happens as pairs orient at metaphase I, and fertilization combines two gametes.

questions.stem: A human cell reaches the end of telophase I. What does each daughter cell contain?
options: 46 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid, so the cell is still diploid.
23 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid, so the cell is already a gamete.
46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, so 92 chromatids in total.
23 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, so 46 chromatids in a haploid cell.
questions.why: Meiosis I halves the set to 23 but does not split centromeres, so each chromosome is still doubled until anaphase II.

questions.stem: Why does a sexual life cycle require both meiosis and fertilization?
options: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and fertilization restores it, so the number stays constant across generations.
Meiosis restores the chromosome number and fertilization halves it before development.
Both halve the number, so the zygote begins with a quarter of the parental set.
Fertilization alone is sufficient; meiosis exists only to make gametes smaller.
questions.why: Without halving, each generation would double the genome; without fusion, the set could never be restored.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte (2n = 46) completes meiosis I normally, forming a secondary oocyte and a first polar body. The secondary oocyte receives 23 chromosomes. What is the chromosome number and ploidy of the first polar body?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes; haploid
distractors: 46 chromosomes; diploid
23 chromosomes; diploid
46 chromosomes; haploid
questions.why: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, so both the secondary oocyte and first polar body receive one chromosome from each pair and are haploid. The 46/23 confusion treats the polar body as a diploid somatic cell.
options: 23 chromosomes; haploid
23 chromosomes; diploid
46 chromosomes; haploid
46 chromosomes; diploid

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human cell shows 47 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome. Which description of this karyotype is correct?
questions.correct: It has 44 autosomes and three sex chromosomes.
distractors: It has 45 autosomes and two sex chromosomes.
It has 46 autosomes and one sex chromosome.
It has 22 autosomes and 25 sex chromosomes.
questions.why: The 47 chromosomes consist of 22 autosome pairs (44 autosomes) plus XXY, so there are three sex chromosomes. A common error is to count the extra chromosome as an autosome instead of recognizing the XXY sex-chromosome set.
options: It has 45 autosomes and two sex chromosomes.
It has 44 autosomes and three sex chromosomes.
It has 22 autosomes and 25 sex chromosomes.
It has 46 autosomes and one sex chromosome.

questions.stem: A diploid organism has 2n = 8. A cell from this organism enters meiosis and is examined in prophase I, after DNA replication. How many homologous pairs and how many chromatids are present in that cell?
questions.correct: 4 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
distractors: 8 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
8 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
questions.why: With 2n = 8 there are four homologous pairs, and replication gives each of the eight chromosomes two chromatids, for 16. The 8-pair choice mistakes individual chromosomes for pairs.
options: 8 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids
8 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 16 chromatids
4 homologous pairs and 8 chromatids

questions.stem: During prophase I, a single crossover occurs between two non-sister chromatids of one homologous pair. After meiosis II, what is the recombinant content of the four chromatids that came from that pair?
questions.correct: Two chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles; two remain nonrecombinant.
distractors: All four chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles.
No chromatids are recombinant because sister chromatids are identical.
All four chromatids carry only paternal alleles.
questions.why: A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids only, so two of the four chromatids become recombinant while the other two stay parental. The all-four choice assumes crossing over affects every chromatid in the pair.
options: No chromatids are recombinant because sister chromatids are identical.
All four chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles.
All four chromatids carry only paternal alleles.
Two chromatids carry a mix of maternal and paternal alleles; two remain nonrecombinant.

questions.stem: A moss sporophyte is diploid and undergoes meiosis to produce spores. A human germ cell is also diploid and undergoes meiosis. How do the products differ in these two life cycles?
questions.correct: Moss meiosis produces haploid spores that grow into a gametophyte; human meiosis produces haploid gametes directly.
distractors: Moss meiosis produces diploid gametes; human meiosis produces haploid spores.
Both produce haploid spores that divide by mitosis into gametes.
Both produce diploid gametes that fuse to form a haploid zygote.
questions.why: In plants, meiosis yields spores and the haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis; in animals, meiosis yields gametes directly. The spore/gamete mix-up is the common plant-versus-animal life-cycle misconception.
options: Moss meiosis produces haploid spores that grow into a gametophyte; human meiosis produces haploid gametes directly.
Moss meiosis produces diploid gametes; human meiosis produces haploid spores.
Both produce haploid spores that divide by mitosis into gametes.
Both produce diploid gametes that fuse to form a haploid zygote.

questions.stem: One human primary spermatocyte (2n = 46) completes meiosis normally. How many sperm are produced, and how many chromosomes does each sperm carry?
questions.correct: Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes
distractors: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
One sperm, with 23 chromosomes
questions.why: Meiosis of one primary spermatocyte yields four haploid sperm, each with 23 chromosomes. The 46-chromosome choice confuses the diploid primary spermatocyte with its haploid products.
options: One sperm, with 23 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes
Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes

questions.stem: In a human male, the X and Y chromosomes differ in size and gene content. What happens to them during meiosis I?
questions.correct: They pair as homologs and separate in anaphase I.
distractors: They do not pair, so both usually go to the same sperm.
They replicate again during meiosis II before separating.
They separate as sister chromatids in anaphase II.
questions.why: X and Y share a small homologous region that allows them to pair and separate like other homologs in meiosis I. The non-pairing choice assumes different sex chromosomes cannot be homologs.
options: They do not pair, so both usually go to the same sperm.
They separate as sister chromatids in anaphase II.
They pair as homologs and separate in anaphase I.
They replicate again during meiosis II before separating.

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II. A sperm enters and triggers completion of meiosis II. What is the immediate result for the oocyte's chromosomes?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids separate, and a second polar body is released.
distractors: Homologous chromosomes separate, and a first polar body is released.
DNA replicates again before the chromosomes separate.
The sperm and oocyte nuclei fuse before meiosis II finishes.
questions.why: Meiosis II resumes at fertilization, separating sister chromatids and producing the ovum plus a second polar body. The homolog-separation choice confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: Homologous chromosomes separate, and a first polar body is released.
DNA replicates again before the chromosomes separate.
The sperm and oocyte nuclei fuse before meiosis II finishes.
Sister chromatids separate, and a second polar body is released.

questions.stem: A technician prepares a human karyotype by blocking cells at metaphase, staining the chromosomes, and arranging them in pairs. Why is metaphase chosen for this procedure?
questions.correct: Chromosomes are condensed and can be seen as distinct bodies.
distractors: Homologous chromosomes have just separated into different cells.
Sister chromatids have just separated and are no longer attached.
Chromosomes are in chromatin form and easier to spread.
questions.why: At metaphase, replicated chromosomes are tightly condensed, making them visible and measurable for pairing. The anaphase choice is wrong because separation would leave each cell with only one of each homolog.
options: Chromosomes are condensed and can be seen as distinct bodies.
Chromosomes are in chromatin form and easier to spread.
Sister chromatids have just separated and are no longer attached.
Homologous chromosomes have just separated into different cells.

questions.stem: Human oogenesis produces one large ovum and small polar bodies from a single primary oocyte. What explains this unequal division?
questions.correct: Cytoplasm is partitioned unequally, so one cell retains most of the resources for the zygote.
distractors: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized.
Meiosis II occurs only in the ovum, not in polar bodies.
Polar bodies contain no chromosomes.
questions.why: Unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis concentrates cytoplasm in the ovum; polar bodies are haploid byproducts. The no-chromosomes choice confuses small size with lacking genetic material.
options: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized.
Cytoplasm is partitioned unequally, so one cell retains most of the resources for the zygote.
Meiosis II occurs only in the ovum, not in polar bodies.
Polar bodies contain no chromosomes.

questions.stem: A student's lab notebook reads: "Crossing over in prophase I creates new alleles, which is why no two gametes are alike." Which statement best corrects this claim?
questions.correct: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles that were already present in the parent cell.
distractors: Crossing over exchanges segments between sister chromatids, which is why each resulting chromatid carries alleles that the parent cell never had.
Crossing over alters the chromosome number of the products, so gametes end up carrying allele combinations absent from the parent cell.
Crossing over generates brand-new alleles at each locus, while independent assortment only shuffles the chromosomes that carry them.
questions.why: Crossing over is a physical swap of homologous segments, so it reshuffles existing alleles rather than creating them; mutation is the source of new alleles. The distractors exploit the common misconception that recombination itself invents alleles.
options: Crossing over exchanges segments between sister chromatids, which is why each resulting chromatid carries alleles that the parent cell never had.
Crossing over alters the chromosome number of the products, so gametes end up carrying allele combinations absent from the parent cell.
Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles that were already present in the parent cell.
Crossing over generates brand-new alleles at each locus, while independent assortment only shuffles the chromosomes that carry them.

questions.stem: In a primary spermatocyte, both sister chromatids of one homolog of chromosome 4 are labeled with a fluorescent dye; the other homolog is unlabeled. The cell completes meiosis normally with no crossing over. How many of the four sperm carry the label?
questions.correct: Two sperm, because the labeled homolog goes to one secondary spermatocyte and its sister chromatids separate into two sperm.
distractors: One sperm, because only one chromatid of the labeled homolog enters a sperm.
Four sperm, because the label is copied to all chromatids during meiosis.
Zero sperm, because the labeled homolog is degraded during meiosis I.
questions.why: The labeled homolog segregates from its partner in meiosis I, then its sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, giving two labeled sperm. The one-sperm choice confuses homolog separation with sister-chromatid separation.
options: Four sperm, because the label is copied to all chromatids during meiosis.
One sperm, because only one chromatid of the labeled homolog enters a sperm.
Zero sperm, because the labeled homolog is degraded during meiosis I.
Two sperm, because the labeled homolog goes to one secondary spermatocyte and its sister chromatids separate into two sperm.

questions.stem: A diploid cell with 2n = 4 is in anaphase I. Cytokinesis has not occurred, so all chromosomes are still in one cell. How many chromosomes are present in that single cell?
questions.correct: Four chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
distractors: Two chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Eight chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
Four chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
questions.why: Homologs have separated toward opposite poles but remain in one cytoplasm, and sister chromatids are still attached, so the cell has four duplicated chromosomes. Counting chromatids as chromosomes gives eight.
options: Four chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Two chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids.
Eight chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.
Four chromosomes, each consisting of one chromatid.

questions.stem: A karyotype prepared from a human shows 45 chromosomes, including one X chromosome and no Y chromosome. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The individual is female with monosomy X, a condition called Turner syndrome.
distractors: The individual is male with Klinefelter syndrome.
The individual is a normal female with 22 autosome pairs.
The individual is female with trisomy X.
questions.why: One X and no Y indicates female, and 45 total chromosomes means one chromosome is missing, matching Turner syndrome (45,X). The distractors swap sex-chromosome constitution or chromosome number.
options: The individual is female with trisomy X.
The individual is female with monosomy X, a condition called Turner syndrome.
The individual is a normal female with 22 autosome pairs.
The individual is male with Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: At birth, a human female's primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I. Each primary oocyte has 46 chromosomes. What is the chromatid content of one such oocyte?
questions.correct: 92 chromatids, because each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids.
distractors: 46 chromatids, because each chromosome has one chromatid before meiosis.
23 chromatids, because meiosis I has already reduced the chromosome number.
92 chromosomes, because DNA replication doubles the chromosome count.
questions.why: The oocyte is diploid and has already replicated its DNA, so each of the 46 chromosomes is duplicated into two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids but still 46 chromosomes. The last distractor assumes replication doubles chromosome number.
options: 23 chromatids, because meiosis I has already reduced the chromosome number.
92 chromosomes, because DNA replication doubles the chromosome count.
92 chromatids, because each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids.
46 chromatids, because each chromosome has one chromatid before meiosis.

questions.stem: A sperm carries two copies of chromosome 7. At a locus near the centromere, one copy has allele A and the other has allele a; no crossing over occurred near that locus. Which meiotic error most likely produced this sperm?
questions.correct: Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes carrying A and a failed to separate.
distractors: Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because sister chromatids carrying A and a failed to separate.
Crossing over in prophase I, because it exchanged A for a between homologs.
Fertilization by two sperm, because each sperm contributed a chromosome 7.
questions.why: The two copies are homologs with different alleles, so they should have separated in meiosis I; meiosis II nondisjunction would produce two identical sister chromatids, not A and a. The meiosis II choice ignores that sisters are identical at that locus.
options: Crossing over in prophase I, because it exchanged A for a between homologs.
Fertilization by two sperm, because each sperm contributed a chromosome 7.
Nondisjunction in meiosis II, because sister chromatids carrying A and a failed to separate.
Nondisjunction in meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes carrying A and a failed to separate.

questions.stem: A drug blocks chiasma formation in a primary spermatocyte, but homologs still align at metaphase I. What is the most likely consequence for the resulting sperm?
questions.correct: Homologs may segregate randomly, producing sperm with abnormal chromosome numbers.
distractors: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so each sperm receives duplicated chromosomes.
DNA replication fails, so each sperm receives half the normal DNA.
Crossing over increases, so all sperm become genetically identical.
questions.why: Chiasmata normally hold homologs together so they orient and separate correctly; without them, homologs can missegregate, causing aneuploid sperm. The distractors confuse chiasmata with sister-chromatid cohesion or replication.
options: Homologs may segregate randomly, producing sperm with abnormal chromosome numbers.
Crossing over increases, so all sperm become genetically identical.
Sister chromatids cannot separate, so each sperm receives duplicated chromosomes.
DNA replication fails, so each sperm receives half the normal DNA.

questions.stem: Colchicine prevents spindle microtubules from forming. A primary oocyte treated with colchicine enters meiosis. What is the most direct effect on chromosome segregation?
questions.correct: Homologs and sister chromatids cannot be pulled apart, so no normal haploid products form.
distractors: Crossing over cannot occur, so homologs remain genetically identical.
DNA replication is blocked, so chromosomes remain unreplicated.
Sister chromatids separate but homologs remain paired, producing diploid gametes.
questions.why: Spindle fibers move chromosomes; without them, segregation fails regardless of crossing over or replication. The distractors wrongly link the spindle to crossing over, replication, or a selective separation.
options: Crossing over cannot occur, so homologs remain genetically identical.
Homologs and sister chromatids cannot be pulled apart, so no normal haploid products form.
DNA replication is blocked, so chromosomes remain unreplicated.
Sister chromatids separate but homologs remain paired, producing diploid gametes.

questions.stem: A human egg with 23 chromosomes is fertilized by two sperm at the same time, and both sperm fuse with the egg. Each sperm has 23 chromosomes. What is the chromosome number of the resulting zygote?
questions.correct: 69 chromosomes, because three haploid sets combine.
distractors: 46 chromosomes, because two sperm replace the missing second gamete.
92 chromosomes, because each sperm doubles after fusion.
23 chromosomes, because the egg's chromosomes are discarded.
questions.why: Fertilization normally combines one haploid egg and one haploid sperm; two sperm add two more haploid sets to the egg's set, giving three sets (69). The distractors miscount the sets or assume chromosome loss or doubling.
options: 92 chromosomes, because each sperm doubles after fusion.
46 chromosomes, because two sperm replace the missing second gamete.
69 chromosomes, because three haploid sets combine.
23 chromosomes, because the egg's chromosomes are discarded.

questions.stem: A student claims that crossing over between sister chromatids during prophase I increases genetic variation. Why is this claim incorrect?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids are identical copies, so exchanging segments between them does not create new allele combinations.
distractors: Sister chromatids are not present in prophase I, so crossing over cannot occur then.
Crossing over between sister chromatids creates new alleles at the break points.
Crossing over only occurs between nonhomologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids.
questions.why: Crossing over generates variation only when non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange different alleles; sister chromatids carry the same alleles, so the exchange is genetically invisible. The distractor about new alleles confuses recombination with mutation.
options: Crossing over only occurs between nonhomologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids.
Crossing over between sister chromatids creates new alleles at the break points.
Sister chromatids are not present in prophase I, so crossing over cannot occur then.
Sister chromatids are identical copies, so exchanging segments between them does not create new allele combinations.

questions.stem: A table gives human cell counts. Which row is inconsistent with normal cell-cycle or meiotic behavior? G1 somatic cell: 46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids. G2 somatic cell: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids. Secondary spermatocyte: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids. Spermatid: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids.
questions.correct: Spermatid, because a spermatid has 23 chromosomes but each chromosome should be a single chromatid.
distractors: G1 somatic cell, because it should have 92 chromatids.
G2 somatic cell, because it should have 46 chromatids.
Secondary spermatocyte, because it should have 46 chromosomes.
questions.why: After meiosis II, spermatids contain 23 unduplicated chromosomes (23 chromatids); 46 chromatids would mean each chromosome is still duplicated. The other rows match expected counts.
options: Spermatid, because a spermatid has 23 chromosomes but each chromosome should be a single chromatid.
G2 somatic cell, because it should have 46 chromatids.
Secondary spermatocyte, because it should have 46 chromosomes.
G1 somatic cell, because it should have 92 chromatids.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a normal human male is arranged in 23 pairs. A student places a label on every chromosome that is not an X or a Y. How many labels are placed?
questions.correct: 44 labels, because there are 22 autosome pairs.
distractors: 46 labels, because all chromosomes are autosomes in a male.
23 labels, because autosomes are counted by pairs rather than individually.
45 labels, because only the Y chromosome is excluded.
questions.why: Autosomes are all chromosomes except sex chromosomes; a male has 22 autosome pairs (44 chromosomes) plus X and Y. The distractors count sex chromosomes as autosomes or count pairs instead of chromosomes.
options: 46 labels, because all chromosomes are autosomes in a male.
44 labels, because there are 22 autosome pairs.
45 labels, because only the Y chromosome is excluded.
23 labels, because autosomes are counted by pairs rather than individually.

questions.stem: A diploid organism has four homologous pairs. Assuming independent assortment and no crossing over, what fraction of its gametes receives the paternal homolog from every pair?
questions.why: Each of the four pairs independently gives a 1/2 chance of the paternal homolog, so (1/2)^4 = 1/16; 1/4 confuses the number of pairs with the probability per pair.

questions.stem: A human karyotype is prepared from a cell arrested at metaphase, so each of the 46 chromosomes is duplicated. How many DNA molecules are displayed in the entire karyotype?
questions.why: At metaphase each chromosome has two sister chromatids, each one DNA molecule, giving 46 × 2 = 92; 46 counts chromosomes rather than chromatids.

questions.stem: A technician tries to arrange chromosomes from a normal human sperm into homologous pairs for a karyotype but cannot. What best explains this failure?
questions.correct: A sperm is haploid, so it carries only one chromosome from each homologous pair.
distractors: A sperm has no chromosomes until fertilization, when they are supplied by the egg.
A sperm's chromosomes are all sex chromosomes, so autosomes cannot be paired.
A sperm has homologous pairs but they are too condensed to recognize.
questions.why: Meiosis reduces the chromosome set to one of each homolog, so a sperm lacks the partner chromosome needed for pairing; the first distractor reverses fertilization's role.
options: A sperm is haploid, so it carries only one chromosome from each homologous pair.
A sperm has homologous pairs but they are too condensed to recognize.
A sperm's chromosomes are all sex chromosomes, so autosomes cannot be paired.
A sperm has no chromosomes until fertilization, when they are supplied by the egg.

questions.stem: A human primary spermatocyte contains one X and one Y chromosome. It completes meiosis normally, producing four sperm. How many of those sperm carry an X chromosome?
questions.correct: Two
distractors: Zero
One
Four
questions.why: The X and Y homologs separate in meiosis I, so two secondary spermatocytes—and their two sperm—receive the X; choosing one assumes sex chromosomes segregate only after meiosis II.
options: Zero
Two
Four
One

questions.stem: A moss gametophyte is haploid and produces gametes by mitosis. A human produces gametes by meiosis. Which comparison of the resulting gametes is correct?
questions.correct: Moss gametes are genetically identical to the gametophyte apart from mutation, while human gametes vary because meiosis shuffles homologs.
distractors: Moss gametes are diploid, while human gametes are haploid because meiosis halves the chromosome number.
Moss gametes vary because mitosis separates homologs, while human gametes are identical to the parent cell.
Both moss and human gametes are produced by meiosis, but moss gametes are larger and therefore diploid.
questions.why: Mitosis in a haploid gametophyte copies the same set, whereas meiosis in humans makes variable haploid gametes; calling moss gametes diploid ignores that the gametophyte is already haploid.
options: Moss gametes are diploid, while human gametes are haploid because meiosis halves the chromosome number.
Moss gametes vary because mitosis separates homologs, while human gametes are identical to the parent cell.
Moss gametes are genetically identical to the gametophyte apart from mutation, while human gametes vary because meiosis shuffles homologs.
Both moss and human gametes are produced by meiosis, but moss gametes are larger and therefore diploid.

questions.stem: A human egg with 23 chromosomes fuses with a normal sperm, forming a zygote. Immediately after fusion, before any DNA replication, how many chromosomes and DNA molecules does the zygote contain?
questions.correct: 46 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules
distractors: 46 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
23 chromosomes and 23 DNA molecules
92 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
questions.why: Fertilization restores 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes, each then a single DNA molecule before S phase; 92 DNA molecules would require replication already.
options: 92 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
46 chromosomes and 92 DNA molecules
23 chromosomes and 23 DNA molecules
46 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules

questions.stem: In a diploid species, one cell is in anaphase II and, before cytokinesis, contains 24 chromosomes. What is the diploid number of this species?
questions.why: At anaphase II sister chromatids separate, so the 24 chromosomes in that cell represent two copies of the haploid set of 12; thus n = 12 and 2n = 24.

questions.stem: A mutant diploid organism is found to have only one set of chromosomes (n = 8) instead of two. It cannot complete meiosis. What is the most direct reason?
questions.correct: It lacks homologous pairs that must synapse and separate in meiosis I.
distractors: It cannot replicate DNA because replication requires two chromosome sets.
Its cells cannot enter mitosis, so meiosis never begins.
It has no centromeres, so sister chromatids cannot attach to spindle fibers.
questions.why: Meiosis I requires homologs to pair and then segregate, and a haploid set has no homolog partners; the replication distractor falsely claims S phase needs two sets.
options: It cannot replicate DNA because replication requires two chromosome sets.
It lacks homologous pairs that must synapse and separate in meiosis I.
It has no centromeres, so sister chromatids cannot attach to spindle fibers.
Its cells cannot enter mitosis, so meiosis never begins.

questions.stem: A tetraploid plant has 4n = 32. It undergoes meiosis to produce gametes. How many chromosomes does each gamete carry?
questions.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number from the tetraploid sporophyte, so gametes receive 32/2 = 16; 8 would be a haploid set of the original diploid, not the tetraploid.

questions.stem: A child's karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with no visible structural abnormalities. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The karyotype does not rule out a single-gene mutation causing the child's disorder.
distractors: The child cannot have a genetic disorder because all chromosomes are present.
The child must have an extra copy of a gene that karyotyping cannot detect.
The child's gametes will all have 23 chromosomes regardless of the child's genotype.
questions.why: Karyotypes reveal chromosome number and large structure, not DNA sequence, so a point mutation can still cause disease; the first distractor treats a normal karyotype as a complete genetic screen.
options: The child must have an extra copy of a gene that karyotyping cannot detect.
The child cannot have a genetic disorder because all chromosomes are present.
The child's gametes will all have 23 chromosomes regardless of the child's genotype.
The karyotype does not rule out a single-gene mutation causing the child's disorder.

questions.stem: A normal human egg is produced. How many autosomes and sex chromosomes does it carry?
questions.correct: 22 autosomes and one X chromosome
distractors: 23 autosomes and one X chromosome
22 autosomes and one Y chromosome
44 autosomes and one X chromosome
questions.why: A human egg is haploid for 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome, and eggs carry X rather than Y; 23 autosomes would incorrectly include a sex chromosome as an autosome.
options: 22 autosomes and one X chromosome
44 autosomes and one X chromosome
23 autosomes and one X chromosome
22 autosomes and one Y chromosome
